ety.text: From Middle English other, from Old English ōþer (“other, second”), from Proto-West Germanic *ą̄þar, *anþar, from Proto-Germanic *anþeraz (“other, second”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énteros (“other”).

ex: Pick up the phone and find out who's on the other end.
I get paid every other week.

senses.d: An other, another (person, etc), more often rendered as another.
ex: I'm afraid little Robbie does not always play well with others.
Show me one other.

senses.d: The other one; the second of two.
ex: One boat is not better than the other.
Why not tell one or other of your parents?

senses.d: Not the one or ones previously referred to.
ex: Earning less than $2,000 a month, I have no other source of income except for gifts from relatives.
“By the way,” Jessamy went on, “what’s your other name? You never told me.” “Stubbs,” said Billy, “William Stubbs!”.
I durst, my lord, to wager she is honest, Lay down my soul at state; if you think other, Remove your thought;

senses.d: To regard, label, or treat as an “other”, as not part of the same group; to view as different and alien.
ex: "Rican" is code for its homonym, "redskin," through which they othered this non-Mexican ethnic group.
Others with admitted addictions are Othered and sadly, forever stigmatized.

senses.d: To treat as different or separate; segregate; ostracise.

grp.label: not the one previously referred to

Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.
Inherited from Latin alter, altera, alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros. Compare Portuguese outro and French autre.

phr: give with one hand and take away with the other
go in at one ear and at out the other

ety.text: From Middle English otherwise, othre wise, from Old English on ōþre wīsan (literally “in (on) other/different manner”); equivalent to other + -wise. Compare West Frisian yn oarwei (“otherwise”), Icelandic öðruvísi (“different”).

ex: Near-synonyms: contrarily, contrastingly
You may have a point, but I think otherwise.
I’m not well today, otherwise I would have helped.
You have to open your umbrella, otherwise you'll get wet.

senses.d: In all other respects; apart from that; except for this.
ex: He lost his temper once in a while. Otherwise he behaved rationally.
There was one rotten apple in an otherwise perfect batch.
He said he didn’t do it, but the evidence was otherwise.
Statistics need lots of information, digital and otherwise.

fr:autrement.gl: differently, in another way or manner

ety.text: From Middle French aultrement, from Old French autrement, from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Synchronically autre + -ment.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Documented since the thirteenth century.

it:differentemente.gl: in a different way, differently, otherwise

chain.g: to carry different ways, spread, scatter, disperse, separate

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin differentem, present active participle of differō (“to differ”).
Contraction of Middle French si non. Compare Catalan sinó, Portuguese senão, and Romanesco "sinnò".
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese senon. By surface analysis, se (“if”) + não (“not”). Compare French sinon, Spanish sino.
From Latin tota via (“always”). Compare Spanish todavía, Portuguese todavia and French toutefois.

ex: I treat others like I treat myself.
Javik: Do not care what others think. Do what you must.

senses.d: Those remaining after one or more people or items have left, or done something else, or been excluded.
ex: Two decided to hide, the others surrendered.
I kept two special jars and threw away all the others.

grp.label: those remaining after something has been excluded

ety.text: Inherited from Latin dē magis; compare Portuguese demais and Asturian demás. Equivalent to de- + más. From Latin magis (“more”) derivative magister comes also English master.

phr: be fearful when others are greedy
be greedy when others are fearful
do unto others as you would have them do unto you
he who digs a pit for others falls in himself
